submission.summary: This 24-year-old female patient has no active General/Surgery problems. Her active problems are Generalized anxiety disorder and Migraine without aura, which are psychiatric and neurological conditions rather than surgical concerns. She was diagnosed with Irritable Bowel Syndrome with Diarrhea (IBS-D) in January 2020 for intermittent crampy abdominal pain and loose stools, but this is not currently listed as an active problem. Her recent encounters include an outpatient visit in 2020 for abdominal symptoms with normal laboratory testing (CBC, CRP, tissue transglutaminase IgA), and an ED visit in July 2021 for altered mental status likely due to benzodiazepine overdose, which responded to flumazenil. Her medications relevant to care include Sertraline 50mg daily for anxiety, Alprazolam 0.25mg PRN for anxiety, Sumatriptan 50mg PRN for migraine, and Ginger extract 500mg PRN for nausea or abdominal cramping. She has no known drug allergies and no history of surgical procedures. From a General/Surgery perspective, this patient has no active surgical conditions, abdominal pathologies, or surgical comorbidities requiring management.

This 45-year-old female patient presents with a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, an active General/Surgery problem requiring surgical resection of a right adrenal mass. The patient's active problem list includes paroxysmal hypertension, which is a manifestation of the underlying pheochromocytoma. She has a significant family history suggestive of MEN2 syndrome, with her father diagnosed with medullary thyroid carcinoma at age 48, her paternal aunt with pheochromocytoma, and her mother with essential hypertension. Laboratory evaluation has revealed markedly elevated plasma and urinary catecholamines and metanephrines, along with elevated serum calcitonin (500 pg/mL) and CEA (10 ng/mL), which may indicate concurrent medullary thyroid carcinoma. Imaging confirms a unilateral adrenal tumor with features concerning for pheochromocytoma. The patient is currently not taking any medications and has no known drug allergies. She has a history of cesarean section and tonsillectomy. Preoperative evaluation has been completed following consultations with Cardiology and Endocrinology over the past year for management of her paroxysmal hypertension symptoms including episodic pounding headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis.

This 65-year-old male with GOLD Stage IV COPD, pulmonary hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and GERD has had multiple recent infectious disease-related encounters. In January 2020, he presented to the ED with shortness of breath, productive cough with yellowish sputum, and fever, with chest X-ray showing right lower lobe consolidation and pleural effusion. In March 2020, he was admitted for worsening respiratory status with somnolence, respiratory acidosis (pH 7.19, PCO2 76 mm Hg), and required increased oxygen support. In July 2020, he was admitted to ICU for severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation. The patient has penicillin (hives) and iodinated contrast (urticaria) allergies, which are critical for infectious disease treatment planning and imaging decisions. His home medications include bronchodilators (albuterol sulfate, tiotropium bromide, fluticasone/salmeterol), home oxygen therapy at 2 liters per minute, lisinopril, metformin, and omeprazole. Laboratory findings include thyroid dysfunction (low T3, elevated reverse T3) and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis from prior normal saline infusion. Family history includes lung cancer and chronic bronchitis in his father, and COPD in his older brother. Social history reveals a 50 pack-year smoking history (quit 3 years ago) and former occupation as a diesel mechanic, both risk factors for respiratory infections.

This 30-year-old female with a history of polycystic ovary syndrome, primary infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and recurrent urinary tract infections presents with recurrent episodes of severe pelvic pain. Her surgical history includes laparoscopic cholecystectomy, laparoscopic drainage of a ruptured ovarian cyst at age 24, and laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy at age 28. She has multiple diagnoses of endometriosis involving the ovaries and bladder, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, and ovarian torsion diagnosed in 2022. Current medications include clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction, naproxen for dysmenorrhea, and prenatal vitamin. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated CA-125 consistent with endometriosis, with normal renal and liver function. Recent transvaginal ultrasound revealed a 5 cm complex ovarian mass with decreased blood flow, concerning for ovarian torsion. She has been managed with ovulation induction therapy for infertility and has experienced multiple emergency department visits for acute pelvic pain episodes.

This 15-year-old female patient has active pulmonology problems including mild persistent asthma and allergic rhinitis, with a history of atopic dermatitis representing the atopic march. She has multiple environmental allergies including dust mites, tree pollen, and grass pollen, plus a significant peanut allergy with anaphylaxis risk. Bronchoalveolar lavage from 2020 demonstrated numerous eosinophils with elevated IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 levels in the airway epithelium, consistent with eosinophilic airway inflammation typical of asthma. The patient has been consistently managed with albuterol inhaler 90 mcg per actuation, 2 puffs every 4-6 hours as needed for wheezing or chest tightness across all encounters. Recent laboratory studies including CBC, thyroid function tests, and electrolytes have been within normal limits, and urine toxicology screens have been negative. Her most recent ED visit in March 2024 was for psychiatric concerns rather than respiratory symptoms, though she maintains her asthma rescue inhaler for symptom management.

This 45-year-old male patient presents with active Hematology/Oncology concerns centered on a suspected malignant neoplasm of the lung, diagnosed in 2020. The patient's oncologic history includes a 6 mm non-calcified nodule discovered on low-dose CT in 2020, which progressed to a 4 cm mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy by 2022, and a centrally located lung mass noted on imaging in January 2024. Comorbidities include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and tobacco use disorder, with a significant 30-pack-year smoking history. Laboratory evaluation from July 2022 demonstrates normal hematologic parameters with hemoglobin 14 g/dL, white blood cell count 7,000/uL, and platelets 250,000/uL, with no evidence of hematologic malignancy or cytopenias. Current medications include tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily and albuterol 90 mcg inhaled every 4-6 hours as needed for shortness of breath, both for COPD management. The patient's recent presentation to the emergency department in January 2024 with progressive confusion, lethargy, poor appetite, and hemoptysis warrants further oncologic evaluation given the known lung mass and constitutional symptoms.

This 5-year-old male has multiple active Medical/Genetics problems including tuberous sclerosis complex, chronic granulomatous disease, and suspected congenital adrenal hyperplasia based on family history. The patient's MRI demonstrates characteristic findings of tuberous sclerosis with multiple cortical tubers and subependymal nodules. Chronic granulomatous disease is suspected to be X-linked based on maternal lineage history of recurrent infections in maternal uncles. The patient has decreased serum DHEA-S and 17-hydroxy-pregnenolone levels, consistent with adrenal insufficiency or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and is currently treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Comorbidities include fetal alcohol syndrome, reactive attachment disorder, recurrent acute otitis media, and gram-negative rod infections with Serratia marcescens. Relevant medications include hydrocortisone 5 mg PO TID, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg PO daily, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for prophylaxis, itraconazole, and levetiracetam. The patient's family history is significant for parental heterozygous carrier status for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and maternal alcohol use disorder.

This 32-year-old male patient has HIV infection (AIDS) as his primary active infectious disease problem, with documented non-adherence to antiretroviral therapy (Biktarvy) for the past 6 months. His CD4 count has been severely suppressed, ranging from 50 to 180 cells/µL, with HIV viral loads consistently elevated at 120,000 copies/mL. He has a significant history of AIDS-defining opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (diagnosed 2020-01-15), Bacillary angiomatosis (diagnosed 2020-10-15, confirmed by pathology showing proliferation of small blood vessels lined by epithelioid endothelial cells), and Cryptosporidiosis (diagnosed 2021-07-15, confirmed by positive stool antigen test). His comorbidities include asthma (managed with albuterol inhaler) and opioid use disorder (in recovery with history of intravenous use). Recent laboratory findings from July 2024 demonstrate leukocytosis (WBC 12,000/µL), lymphopenia (15%), thrombocytopenia (platelets 150,000/µL), elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 80 mg/L), and significant hypoxemia (PaO2 55 mmHg on room air). He was recently admitted to the Infectious Diseases department in July 2024 with high-grade fever, cough, and difficulty breathing after returning from a country with an ongoing outbreak of a highly contagious respiratory virus, with chest X-ray showing bilateral interstitial infiltrates.

This 58-year-old male patient has active cardiology problems including hypertension and hyperlipidemia, with a significant history of acute myocardial infarction diagnosed in July 2020 and stable angina pectoris due to coronary artery disease diagnosed in January 2021. His cardiology-relevant comorbidities include bipolar I disorder, obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP therapy, and stage II colorectal adenocarcinoma status post hemicolectomy. Current cardiology medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily for blood pressure control and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for lipid management. His most recent lipid panel demonstrates LDL of 98 mg/dL, HDL of 45 mg/dL, and triglycerides of 150 mg/dL, with blood pressures consistently in the 130s/80s range. Cardiac imaging from January 2021 revealed a reversible defect in the anterior wall on SPECT myocardial perfusion imaging, indicating myocardial ischemia. The patient has a strong family history of cardiovascular disease, including paternal myocardial infarction at age 55 and paternal uncle's ischemic stroke at age 60. He is a never-smoker with social alcohol use and maintains a healthy diet. His cardiac care focuses on secondary prevention of myocardial infarction and management of coronary artery disease.

This 22-year-old male construction laborer presents with a history of multiple traumatic events requiring emergency care. His active Emergency/Medicine problems include traumatic hemothorax with hypovolemic shock (diagnosed 2020-01-15 following a stab wound to the left chest) and unstable pelvic fracture (diagnosed 2020-09-15 after a high-speed motor vehicle collision). The patient has no current active problems listed in the problem list, but these traumatic injuries remain relevant comorbidities for Emergency/Medicine care. Laboratory findings demonstrate significant anemia with hemoglobin levels dropping from a baseline of 14 g/dL to 8-9 g/dL across encounters, consistent with ongoing blood loss from his injuries. The patient takes no medications and has no known drug allergies. Social history reveals current daily smoking (1 pack/day for 3 years) and heavy episodic alcohol use (3-4 times weekly), which are relevant risk factors for his overall health. Recent encounters show recurrent presentations for trauma, including a 2021 head-on motor vehicle collision with signs of hemorrhagic shock requiring ICU admission.

This 52-year-old female with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presents with significant gastroenterology concerns centered on non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and hepatic adenoma. She underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 45 and recently presented to the ED in January 2024 with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting 5 days post-cholecystectomy, accompanied by fever (38.3°C), tachycardia (110 bpm), and leukocytosis (WBC 16,000/mm³). Her liver function tests demonstrate chronic elevation with AST 52-85 U/L and ALT 63-85 U/L, consistent with NASH, and hepatitis serologies are negative. Abdominal ultrasound in 2022 confirmed hepatic steatosis without gallstones or biliary ductal dilatation. Her metabolic profile shows persistent hyperglycemia with HbA1c 7.2-7.9%, elevated triglycerides (250-260 mg/dL), and LDL cholesterol 130-158 mg/dL. Current medications include metformin 1000 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and lisinopril 20 mg daily. She has no alcohol use and is non-smoker, supporting the diagnosis of metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease.

This 70-year-old male patient presents with lower urinary tract symptoms including progressive urinary frequency, urgency, weak stream, and nocturia, consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). His urology encounter from January 2020 revealed a uniformly enlarged, smooth, nontender prostate on digital rectal examination with mildly elevated postvoid residual volume. The patient is currently taking tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly for BPH management. His active medical problems include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease (stable angina), and giant cell arteritis, with the latter requiring prednisone 10 mg daily which may have renal implications. Renal function has been monitored over time with serum creatinine levels ranging from 1.0 to 1.8 mg/dL, with a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis was unremarkable in 2020 but showed microscopic hematuria in March 2021. The patient has no active urology-specific problems listed, but his BPH and LUTS are being managed. Comorbidities relevant to urology care include hypertension (affecting renal function), and the family history of abdominal aortic aneurysm in his maternal uncle.

This 67-year-old male with a 40-45 pack-year smoking history presents with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and tobacco use disorder as his primary pulmonology problems. He has a significant comorbidity burden including hypertension, hyperlipidemia, peripheral arterial disease, and age-related macular degeneration. His pulmonary function testing demonstrates severe obstructive lung disease with FEV1/FVC ratios of 31-60% and FEV1 of 40-45% of predicted values. Oxygen saturation has been consistently 92% on room air. Most concerning is the evolution of a solitary pulmonary nodule (1.2 cm with spiculated margins in the right upper lobe) identified in January 2023, which progressed to a right hilar mass by July 2023, raising high suspicion for lung malignancy. His current medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension; atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia; and aspirin for cardiovascular risk reduction. Recent imaging findings and his smoking history warrant urgent oncologic evaluation for the pulmonary mass.

This 53-year-old male patient has severe alcohol use disorder as his primary active problem, with no active cardiology-specific diagnoses. However, from a cardiology perspective, several comorbidities and findings are highly relevant: he has hypomagnesemia (diagnosed 2020-04-15) and hypocalcemia (serum calcium 7.1 mg/dL), both of which can predispose to arrhythmias. His ECG demonstrates a prolonged QT interval, increasing risk for torsades de pointes and other ventricular arrhythmias. He is currently taking magnesium oxide 400 mg twice daily for hypomagnesemia. Additional cardiac risk factors include a 35-pack-year smoking history and family history of hypertension in his sister. His GERD with chronic aspiration risk and protein-energy malnutrition may contribute to cardiac stress. He is also on mirtazapine for major depressive disorder, which can affect cardiac conduction. Laboratory findings show mild hyponatremia (135 mEq/L) and history of tachycardia (HR 102 bpm). The patient's alcohol use disorder places him at risk for alcoholic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, requiring careful monitoring of electrolytes and cardiac function.

This 78-year-old female patient with a history of Alzheimer's disease and Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features presents with recurrent psychiatric symptoms requiring emergency evaluation. Her active psychiatric problems include Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features (diagnosed 2025-01-15) and Alzheimer's disease (diagnosed 2021-07-15), which manifests with progressive cognitive decline, memory impairment, and behavioral disturbances including agitation and combative behavior. Comorbid medical conditions include Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (A1c 7.2%), Hyperlipidemia, and Essential Hypertension. Laboratory evaluation shows normal thyroid function (TSH 2.5 μIU/mL), normal electrolytes, and no evidence of metabolic derangements contributing to her psychiatric symptoms. Current medications include sertraline for depression, metformin for diabetes, lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension, simvastatin for hyperlipidemia, and aspirin. The patient's psychiatric care should address both her mood disorder and the behavioral symptoms associated with her Alzheimer's disease, while monitoring for medication interactions and metabolic complications.

This 4-year-old female patient was evaluated in Pediatric Rheumatology in January 2020 for a 2-month history of intermittent fever, right knee swelling, and morning limping. Physical examination revealed a warm, swollen right knee with limited range of motion. Laboratory studies demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers with ESR of 40 mm/hr (normal 0-20 mm/hr) and CRP of 2.5 mg/dL (normal <0.8 mg/dL), along with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) and negative rheumatoid factor. The patient has a family history of autoimmune conditions, including maternal autoimmune hypothyroidism and maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis. She is currently being treated with Naproxen suspension 125 mg orally twice daily with food for anti-inflammatory management. No known drug allergies are documented. The patient's active problem list is currently empty, suggesting the inflammatory condition may have resolved or been managed. A follow-up routine check-up was performed in July 2020 in General Pediatrics.

This 32-year-old Hispanic male presents to the Emergency Department with weakness in his right arm and leg following a motorcycle accident. His active Emergency/Medicine problem is a spinal cord injury at the T10 level, evidenced by a hyperintense lesion on spinal MRI involving the right half of the spinal cord, resulting in decreased strength (3/5), diminished proprioception and vibratory sensation, and decreased light touch on the right side. The patient has no active problems listed in his problem list and takes no medications. His comorbidities include a history of compartment syndrome of the right hand requiring fasciotomy in 2020, high-pressure injection injury of the left hand diagnosed in 2020, and left lower leg embolectomy following traumatic vascular injury in 2020. Relevant labs from his most recent encounter show normal CBC, electrolytes, and toxicology screen. Previous encounters demonstrate elevated CK (2500 U/L) and myoglobin (150 ng/mL) during his 2020 lower leg injury, consistent with rhabdomyolysis. He is a former smoker who quit 6 months ago with social alcohol use, and has no known drug allergies.

This 27-year-old female patient presents with a diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma, confirmed by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells on lymph node biopsy. The patient initially presented in January 2020 with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and 5 kg weight loss. Subsequent evaluation in February 2020 at Hematology & Oncology confirmed the diagnosis with characteristic B symptoms and a palpable supraclavicular lymph node. Laboratory studies demonstrate elevated inflammatory markers including ESR of 50 mm/hr and LDH ranging from 245-350 U/L, with eosinophilia (10%) noted on the most recent visit. Imaging reveals a mediastinal mass on chest radiograph, consistent with nodal involvement. The patient has not yet received any chemotherapy or other treatment, as she currently takes no medications. Family history is notable for a paternal cousin with Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed at age 26. Physical examination demonstrates persistent lymphadenopathy in cervical and axillary regions with no other significant comorbidities. The clinical picture is consistent with classic Hodgkin lymphoma requiring further staging and treatment planning.

This 17-year-old female with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and complex eating disorder history presented to the Emergency Department with multiple concerning episodes. Her active Emergency/Medicine problems include Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus with poor insulin compliance, secondary amenorrhea, and history of refeeding syndrome. She has comorbidities of anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, Female Athlete Triad, and hyperphosphatemia. Recent laboratory findings from 2025-01-15 reveal severe hyperglycemia (450 mg/dL), elevated HbA1c (12%), metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 18 mEq/L), elevated BUN (30 mg/dL), and 4+ ketones on urinalysis, consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis. Historical ED encounters in 2022 documented syncope, collapse, and weakness with electrolyte abnormalities including hypokalemia (3.0-3.2 mEq/L), hyponatremia (132 mEq/L), and metabolic alkalosis. Current medications include insulin glargine and lispro (both noncompliant due to fear of injections), fluoxetine 20 mg daily, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and calcium carbonate 600 mg three times daily. Physical examination shows cachexia, dehydration, and BMI of 16. The patient's clinical picture represents a high-risk scenario with life-threatening metabolic derangements requiring urgent stabilization and multidisciplinary management.

This 62-year-old female patient has active orthopedic concerns centered on metastatic breast cancer with osseous metastases and a history of left total knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis. Her active orthopedic problems include metastatic breast cancer (invasive ductal carcinoma) with bone metastases, multiple myeloma or metastatic bone disease requiring intravenous bisphosphonates, and osteoarthritis of the left knee status post total knee arthroplasty. Relevant comorbidities significantly impact orthopedic care, including chronic kidney disease stage 4 with secondary hyperparathyroidism, type 2 diabetes mellitus with polyneuropathy, and hyperlipidemia. Laboratory findings demonstrate malignancy-associated hypercalcemia with elevated calcium levels (up to 13.4 mg/dL), elevated phosphorus (6.8 mg/dL), and markedly elevated PTH (600 pg/mL) consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Imaging reveals a lytic lesion of the mid-shaft of the humerus, consistent with metastatic bone disease. Medications relevant to orthopedic care include acetaminophen for pain management, anastrozole for hormone suppression therapy of breast cancer, calcitriol for secondary hyperparathyroidism, sevelamer carbonate for CKD management, and atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. The patient has no known drug allergies and is currently being managed with a comprehensive approach to bone health and metastatic disease.

This 35-year-old male with history of multiple traumatic injuries (healed rib fractures, resolved pulmonary contusion, and mild traumatic brain injury) presents with several active Emergency/Medicine concerns. He was diagnosed with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia in March 2021 following a motor vehicle accident, confirmed by chest x-ray showing bowel loops in the left thoracic cavity with mediastinal shift. He also has cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea diagnosed in April 2020, confirmed by elevated protein and positive beta-2 transferrin in nasal discharge. In January 2022, he was admitted to ICU with fever, headache, confusion, and tingling at a bat scratch site from two months prior, with CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis suggestive of rabies or other bat-related infection. His medications are limited to a daily multivitamin, and he has no known drug allergies. He is a never-smoker and social drinker who works as a wildlife photographer. Laboratory studies during his recent encounters have been largely within normal limits, with the exception of the CSF findings in the 2022 ICU admission.

This 67-year-old male patient has diverticulosis of the colon diagnosed in 2020, which was an incidental finding during his infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm open repair. He has never undergone colonoscopy and denies prior gastrointestinal bleeding, changes in bowel habits, abdominal pain, or unexplained weight loss. From a Gastroenterology perspective, his active GI problem is limited to diverticulosis of the colon, with no evidence of active diverticulitis or other GI pathology. The patient has significant cardiovascular comorbidities including hypertension (poorly controlled), hyperlipidemia, peripheral artery disease, coronary artery disease, history of cerebrovascular disease, and recent myocardial infarctions. He is currently taking aspirin 81 mg daily, which increases his risk for GI bleeding, particularly in the setting of diverticulosis. His medications also include atorvastatin, lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. Laboratory evaluation shows normal hemoglobin (14.1 g/dL) and platelets (250 x 10^3/uL), with no evidence of anemia or thrombocytopenia. Recent cardiac markers were elevated consistent with his recent MI diagnoses. No liver function tests or other GI-specific laboratory abnormalities are documented. The patient's overall management should consider his GI bleeding risk from aspirin use in the context of his cardiovascular needs.

This 28-year-old Hispanic female patient presents with significant Obstetrics/Gynecology concerns including preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) and chorioamnionitis diagnosed in January 2020. Her active problems include generalized anxiety disorder, hypothyroidism, and iron deficiency anemia, all of which are relevant to her obstetric care. The patient was admitted for PPROM with confirmed amniotic fluid leakage via nitrazine test and ferning, with ultrasound showing an amniotic fluid index of 3 cm. She subsequently developed chorioamnionitis evidenced by fever (38.7°C), tachycardia (110 bpm), uterine tenderness, and elevated inflammatory markers including WBC of 18,000/mm³ and CRP of 24 mg/L. Her hemoglobin of 12.2 g/dL is consistent with her iron deficiency anemia. Medications relevant to OBGYN care include prenatal vitamin with iron for anemia management, levothyroxine 88 mcg daily for hypothyroidism, sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety, and docusate sodium PRN for constipation. She has significant allergies to penicillin (anaphylaxis) and latex (contact dermatitis), which are critical considerations for obstetric care. The patient delivered at term in January 2021 via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a full-term male infant. Family history includes maternal history of PPROM and a sister with chorioamnionitis, suggesting potential genetic or environmental risk factors for pregnancy complications.

This 46-year-old male patient with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 presented to Neurology outpatient clinic with progressive numbness and tingling in hands and feet for 8 months, accompanied by mild weakness climbing stairs and difficulty with fine motor tasks. His active neurology problem is Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2, a hereditary neuropathy, supported by nerve conduction studies showing slowed conduction velocities in both sensory and motor nerves of upper and lower extremities, along with physical exam findings of reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in stocking-glove distribution, mild distal muscle weakness in lower limbs, and absent ankle reflexes. Family history is notable for a brother diagnosed with a hereditary neuropathy in his 30s. Comorbidities include dyslipidemia and elevated blood pressure, which are managed with atorvastatin 20 mg daily and gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, respectively. The patient has no history of diabetes, alcohol use disorder, or recent infections that could confound the neuropathy diagnosis. Recent laboratory results from 2020 show total cholesterol 195 mg/dL, LDL 120 mg/dL, HDL 55 mg/dL, triglycerides 100 mg/dL, and fasting glucose 88 mg/dL, indicating well-controlled dyslipidemia. The patient is a never-smoker with social alcohol use (1-2 drinks per week) and works as a high school mathematics teacher.

This 34-year-old male with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), diagnosed in 2020, presents to the ED with epigastric discomfort and dark stools. His active problem list includes Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) and Tobacco use disorder, but ADPKD remains a significant nephrology concern requiring ongoing monitoring. The patient has a strong family history of ADPKD with his father having end-stage renal disease. Current nephrology-relevant findings include serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL (within normal range) and abdominal ultrasound demonstrating multiple bilateral renal cysts. He has no personal history of diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia, which are common comorbidities that could accelerate renal disease progression. Medications include albuterol inhaler for dyspnea and occasional ibuprofen use, which may pose nephrotoxic risk in the setting of ADPKD and should be minimized. The patient continues to smoke one pack of cigarettes daily, a significant risk factor that could accelerate renal disease progression and complicate management. Given his young age and ADPKD diagnosis, regular nephrology follow-up with monitoring of renal function, blood pressure, and cyst progression is warranted.

This 37-year-old African American male has a history of nephrotic syndrome diagnosed during a 2020 nephrology outpatient visit for 2-month history of fatigue and bilateral leg swelling. Physical examination at that time revealed periorbital edema and 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. Urinalysis demonstrated 4+ protein and oval fat bodies under polarized light, consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Serum studies showed hypoalbuminemia (2.5 g/dL) and hyperlipidemia (total cholesterol 300 mg/dL), while creatinine was normal at 1.0 mg/dL. Renal biopsy revealed scattered areas of sclerosis and hyalinosis involving some glomeruli without complement protein or immunoglobulin deposits, suggestive of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). The patient has a family history of end-stage renal disease in his paternal uncle. Currently, the patient has no active nephrology problems listed, with normal renal function. His current medications include cetirizine 10 mg PO daily as needed for seasonal allergic rhinitis, which is not nephrology-related. No nephrology-specific medications are currently prescribed.

This 17-year-old female patient has Type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed on 2020-01-15, with a history of three recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) admissions in 2020 and 2021. Her active endocrinology problem is Type 1 diabetes mellitus, complicated by recurrent DKA episodes characterized by severe hyperglycemia (blood glucose 480-550 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 10-12 mEq/L, anion gap 25 mEq/L), and significant ketonuria (4+ ketones). Current medications include insulin glargine 24 units subcutaneous at bedtime for basal coverage and insulin lispro sliding scale (1 unit per 10g carbohydrates) for prandial coverage. Family history is notable for maternal autoimmune hypothyroidism and paternal type 2 diabetes mellitus, consistent with autoimmune diathesis. The patient's recent ICU admission in July 2022 for suspected meningococcal meningitis (CSF: WBC 2,000/mm³, glucose 20 mg/dL, Gram-negative diplococci) may be related to her recurrent DKA and potential immune dysfunction. No other active endocrinology comorbidities are documented. Management should focus on optimizing insulin dosing, addressing adherence issues, and preventing future DKA episodes through education and monitoring.

This 25-year-old male patient presents with active psychiatric diagnoses of Schizotypal Personality Disorder (diagnosed 2020) and Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features (diagnosed 2022). He has a significant family history of psychiatric illness including paternal Bipolar I Disorder, maternal Major Depressive Disorder, and paternal uncle with schizophrenia. The patient is currently maintained on Lithium carbonate 300 mg PO BID and Lamotrigine 100 mg PO daily for mood stabilization. His psychiatric history includes multiple ED visits for acute manic episodes with psychotic features, characterized by decreased sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, and paranoid ideation. In January 2025, he was admitted for acute mania and subsequently developed an acute dystonic reaction (neck pain, facial tightness, oculogyric crisis) approximately 5 hours after initiating a new high-potency antipsychotic medication. Laboratory workup including complete blood count, thyroid function tests, and urine toxicology screens have been consistently negative. He has no known drug allergies and no significant medical comorbidities. His social history reveals he is a graduate student in Electrical Engineering who is a nonsmoker with occasional social alcohol use.

This 26-year-old female patient has a history of acute urticaria diagnosed in January 2020, presenting with pruritic, raised, erythematous wheals on her trunk and arms. The lesions were described as well-demarcated erythematous plaques with pale halos that came and went, with individual spots resolving within a day. She was evaluated again in September 2020 with similar symptoms, and acute urticaria was listed as an active problem at that time. Laboratory workup including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and serum tryptase were all within normal limits. The patient has no known drug allergies, takes no medications, and has no current active dermatology problems. Family history includes maternal seasonal allergic rhinitis and paternal asthma. Social history is notable for being a never smoker with social alcohol use. From a dermatology perspective, this patient has no active dermatology problems currently, with only a history of resolved acute urticaria.

This 38-year-old male patient presents with recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis as the primary active nephrology problem. He was diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism in January 2020, which is a significant comorbidity contributing to his nephrolithiasis. The patient has experienced multiple episodes of calcium oxalate kidney stones over the past five years, with at least two requiring emergency department visits. Laboratory evaluation in 2020 revealed elevated serum calcium (11.2 mg/dL) with normal phosphate and 25-D3 levels. More recent testing in 2022 demonstrated elevated urinary calcium excretion with normal serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels. The patient is currently not taking any medications and has no known drug allergies. Family history is positive for kidney stones in his father and primary hyperparathyroidism in his paternal aunt. He maintains a balanced diet and adequate fluid intake of approximately 2 liters daily. Physical examination in 2020 noted mild muscle weakness in the upper and lower extremities, consistent with hypercalcemia symptoms. The patient is a never smoker with social alcohol use and works as a software engineer.

This 51-year-old male patient presents with two active cardiology-related problems: essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He is currently managed with amlodipine 5 mg PO daily for hypertension and rosuvastatin 10 mg PO daily for hyperlipidemia. Family history is significant for cardiovascular disease, with his father experiencing a myocardial infarction at age 68 and hypertension. The patient has several comorbidities including chronic mechanical low back pain, seasonal allergic rhinitis, arsenic toxicity (diagnosed in 2020, likely related to occupational exposure to pressure-treated wood in construction), and a hematologic malignancy (hairy cell leukemia based on TRAP-positive abnormal cells). Laboratory findings demonstrate anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 80,000-100,000/µL), leukopenia (WBC 2,000-2,900/µL), and elevated liver enzymes (AST 52 U/L, ALT 48 U/L). The patient has no documented history of acute coronary syndrome, heart failure, or other specific cardiac conditions. His cardiovascular risk profile is elevated due to hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and family history of premature coronary artery disease.

This 28-year-old male has a history of multiple traumatic injuries with orthopedic significance, including a right clavicular fracture diagnosed in January 2020 following a bicycle accident and a deformed femur noted in July 2021 after a severe motor vehicle collision. The patient's problem list is currently empty, but the femoral deformity represents an ongoing orthopedic concern requiring evaluation. There are no current medications, and the patient is NKDA. Laboratory findings reveal severe anemia with hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL and hematocrit 18%, which is clinically significant for orthopedic surgical planning. The patient is a Jehovah's Witness who refuses blood transfusions, a critical consideration for any orthopedic interventions. Family history includes paternal hypertension and maternal hypothyroidism, with no known family history of bleeding disorders or connective tissue disorders. The patient's occupation as a gig economy driver/cyclist places him at increased risk for future orthopedic injuries. Social history notes occasional social alcohol use and never-smoker status. No active comorbidities are listed that would specifically impact orthopedic care beyond the anemia and religious restrictions.

This 28-year-old female patient presents with active dermatology problems including hidradenitis suppurativa (diagnosed March 2020), acne, and progressive hair thinning on the crown of her head. She has significant comorbidities relevant to dermatology care, including polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosed in January 2020, which is strongly associated with her hirsutism (excess facial hair with male distribution pattern), acne, and alopecia. Obesity (BMI 36 kg/m²) is also present and contributes to hidradenitis suppurativa pathophysiology and overall skin health considerations. Her laboratory evaluation reveals elevated total testosterone (82 ng/dL, normal 8-60 ng/dL) consistent with PCOS, with normal TSH (2.5 µIU/mL) ruling out thyroid dysfunction as a cause of hair loss. Current medications directly relevant to dermatology include clindamycin phosphate 1% topical gel BID for acne and HS lesions, and metformin 1000 mg PO BID for PCOS management which also helps with acne and hirsutism. She has no drug allergies and is on nitrofurantoin for UTI prophylaxis and dicyclomine PRN for abdominal cramping. Her past medical history includes laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 26 and a family history of PCOS in her sister.

This 66-year-old male with a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease presented to the ICU in January 2024 with agitation, confusion, severe headache, and flushed appearance 48 hours after admission for hypertensive emergency. His most recent laboratory evaluation on 2024-01-15 revealed elevated serum creatinine of 2.8 mg/dL (baseline 2.5 mg/dL) and BUN of 55 mg/dL, indicating worsening renal function. The patient has been on sodium nitroprusside infusion, and the clinical picture suggests potential cyanide toxicity. His active nephrology problems include chronic kidney disease and hypertension, which are poorly controlled with blood pressure readings of 145/90 mmHg. Relevant comorbidities include benign prostatic hyperplasia with urethral stricture (diagnosed 2023-01-15), primary myelofibrosis (diagnosed 2021-01-15) with pancytopenia and splenomegaly, and Paget disease of bone. Medications relevant to nephrology care include hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily for blood pressure control, plus tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for BPH. Previous laboratory data from 2023-01-15 showed creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL with hematuria on urinalysis, while 2020-07-15 labs demonstrated normal calcium-phosphate metabolism with elevated alkaline phosphatase (220 U/L) and normal PTH (55 pg/mL). The patient has no drug allergies and is a former smoker with 40 pack-year history.

This 27-year-old female patient presents with a complex hematologic profile characterized by chronic iron deficiency anemia secondary to heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) since menarche, and acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) diagnosed in 2020. Her active hematologic problems include iron deficiency anemia with documented hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL on multiple occasions, and AIP which is a rare autosomal dominant metabolic disorder affecting heme synthesis. Laboratory evidence of hemolysis is present, including elevated reticulocyte count (8%), elevated indirect bilirubin (3.2 mg/dL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and undetectable haptoglobin, consistent with AIP-related hemolytic anemia. Physical examination findings of scleral icterus, mild splenomegaly, and decreased pinprick sensation in a stocking-glove distribution support the diagnosis of AIP with neuropathy. Comorbidities contributing to her hematologic status include restrictive eating behavior with frequent meal skipping, which may exacerbate nutritional deficiencies, and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. Her current medications include a multivitamin with iron taken sporadically and ibuprofen for menstrual cramps, though iron supplementation adherence appears suboptimal. Family history is significant for maternal grandmother with AIP, suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance. The patient's anemia is multifactorial, driven by chronic blood loss from menorrhagia, poor iron intake from restrictive eating, and hemolysis from AIP.

This 70-year-old male patient has active Cardiology problems including paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and hypertension. His comorbidities include Parkinson's disease (7-year duration), Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (long-standing, poorly controlled), chronic migraine, and neurogenic bladder secondary to sacral nerve root injury. The patient has a significant cardiac history, including a 2024-01-15 ICU admission for suspected aortic dissection presenting with tearing chest pain radiating to the back, syncope, and a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray. Physical examination at that time revealed a diastolic murmur at the right second intercostal space and a blood pressure differential between arms (180/95 mmHg right vs 165/90 mmHg left), with a family history of abdominal aortic aneurysm (mother had AAA repair at age 72). Relevant Cardiology medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily for hypertension, apixaban 5 mg BID and aspirin 81 mg daily for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, and metformin 1000 mg BID for diabetes management. Laboratory evaluation during the aortic dissection workup showed normal troponin I (<0.04 ng/mL), with recent labs demonstrating mild hypokalemia (potassium 3.2 mEq/L) and normal renal function (creatinine 1.0-1.1 mg/dL). The patient is currently on dual anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy for his atrial fibrillation, which requires careful monitoring given his complex medical history.

This 64-year-old male with a 25-year history of poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and hypertension presents with chronic kidney disease diagnosed in 2021. His nephrology-relevant active problems include chronic kidney disease, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, hypertension, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, diabetic retinopathy, and hyperlipidemia. At his 2021 nephrology encounter, laboratory evaluation revealed elevated serum creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL, elevated BUN of 36 mg/dL, hyperkalemia at 5.5 mEq/L, and anemia with hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL. Current medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily for blood pressure and renal protection, metformin 1000 mg BID, insulin glargine 30 units at bedtime, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. His diabetes remains poorly controlled with an HbA1c of 9.2% as of July 2025. The patient also has neurogenic bladder due to sacral nerve root injury, which complicates his urinary symptoms. Comorbidities including gastric adenocarcinoma diagnosed in January 2025 and vitamin B12 deficiency further complicate his clinical picture. Management should focus on optimizing glycemic control, managing blood pressure, monitoring renal function, and addressing anemia and hyperkalemia in the context of his CKD.

This 72-year-old male with history of mechanical mitral valve replacement, severe aortic stenosis, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease (Stage 3), chronic constipation, and history of colonic polyps presents with recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding. His active gastroenterology problems include gastrointestinal angiodysplasia with hemorrhage (diagnosed 2022-01-15) and iron deficiency anemia (diagnosed 2022-07-15). The patient has experienced multiple episodes of rectal bleeding, including bright red blood per rectum and maroon-colored stools, with hemoglobin levels consistently in the 9.2-9.8 g/dL range. Gastrointestinal angiodysplasia was identified in the cecum during colonoscopy during active bleeding, showing small, flat, cherry-red lesions with ectatic vessels. The patient is on warfarin 5 mg daily (INR goal 2.5-3.5 for mechanical valve) and aspirin 81 mg daily, both of which increase bleeding risk. Additional medications include metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and amlodipine. Laboratory findings demonstrate chronic iron deficiency with ferritin 15 ng/mL and microcytic anemia (MCV 72-89 fL). INR was subtherapeutic at 1.0 during the most recent ED visit, and BUN was elevated at 28 mg/dL, consistent with upper GI bleeding or chronic GI blood loss. Despite multiple colonoscopies and an abdominal CT angiography, the bleeding source was initially elusive until angiodysplasia was identified.

This 40-year-old Hispanic male presents with active orthopedic problems including chronic mechanical low back pain and S1 radiculopathy, diagnosed in January 2020. He recently presented to the ED in July 2020 with sudden-onset low back pain while lifting heavy boxes, with pain radiating down the posterior aspect of his left leg to the lateral foot. Physical examination revealed a positive straight leg raise on the left at 30 degrees, decreased sensation over the lateral aspect of the left foot, mild weakness with plantar flexion, and diminished left Achilles reflex, consistent with S1 radiculopathy. His comorbidities include obesity (BMI 32), which is a significant risk factor for orthopedic issues, and essential hypertension. Relevant surgical history includes right knee arthroscopy for meniscal tear in 2018. Family history is notable for maternal uncle with lumbar disc herniation requiring discectomy. Current medications include lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, and acetaminophen 500 mg PRN for headaches. No lab or imaging results are available in the record.

This 25-year-old female patient has a history of recurrent bacterial vaginosis, first diagnosed in January 2020 with characteristic findings of thin, malodorous vaginal discharge, elevated vaginal pH (5.5), positive KOH whiff test, and clue cells on wet mount microscopy. She presented to the emergency department in January 2021 with a 3-day history of sore throat, fever (peaking at 38.9°C), and lower abdominal pain, which she attributed to unprotected oral sex with a new partner. Physical examination revealed an erythematous throat without exudates, bilateral lower abdominal tenderness, and mucopurulent cervical discharge, raising concern for possible sexually transmitted infection. Laboratory evaluation showed an unremarkable urinalysis, negative rapid strep test, and nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) was performed on both pharyngeal and cervical specimens. The patient has no current medications, no known drug allergies, and her comorbidities include prior tonsillectomy and wisdom teeth extraction. Family history is notable for maternal hypertension and paternal type 2 diabetes mellitus. She is sexually active with multiple partners and inconsistently uses barrier protection, which may contribute to her recurrent infections.

This 54-year-old female patient has Hypertension as her only active Cardiology problem. She has significant comorbidities including Type 2 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis, which are relevant to cardiovascular risk stratification. Her current medications include lisinopril for hypertension management, metformin for diabetes, and chronic prednisone therapy for rheumatoid arthritis. Laboratory findings demonstrate hyperkalemia (potassium 5.5 mEq/L) and elevated creatinine (1.2 mg/dL), which are important considerations given her ACE inhibitor therapy and potential renal impairment. Hyponatremia (sodium 130 mEq/L) is also noted. Recent encounters reveal episodes of hypotension (BP 85/50 mmHg) and tachycardia (HR 110 bpm), which may be related to her underlying conditions or medications. There is no evidence of active coronary artery disease, arrhythmias, or heart failure in the chart. A DVT was diagnosed in 2020, which is a thrombotic risk factor relevant to cardiovascular care. The patient's elevated D-dimer in 2020 further supports thrombotic risk. Overall, from a Cardiology perspective, this patient requires ongoing management of hypertension with attention to renal function and electrolyte abnormalities, particularly in the context of her diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.

This 52-year-old female with a history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast (ER+, PR+, HER2-) diagnosed in 2022 presents with multiple comorbidities relevant to hematology/oncology care. Her active hematology/oncology problem is the history of breast cancer, though there is no evidence of current active treatment or disease monitoring. Significant comorbidities include end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis for 9 years, post-surgical hypoparathyroidism, poorly controlled hypertension, hepatitis C infection (positive antibody and RNA), and history of intravenous drug use in remission for 5 years. Relevant laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, elevated PTH levels, low serum calcium, and high phosphate consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Current medications include amlodipine, sevelamer carbonate, calcium acetate, calcitriol, levothyroxine, acetaminophen, and docusate sodium, with no evidence of current chemotherapy or targeted therapy for the breast cancer. The patient's most recent encounters have been for other conditions including syncopal episode, fatigue, and skin lesions, with no specific hematology/oncology follow-up noted.

This 50-year-old male patient has several active Gastroenterology-relevant problems including achalasia (diagnosed 2021-03-15), alcohol use disorder (diagnosed 2021-09-15), and folate deficiency anemia (diagnosed 2022-03-15). The patient has a significant history of heavy alcohol consumption (6-8 beers daily for 10 years) with a family history of alcohol use disorder. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly with the liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, though no jaundice, ascites, or spider angiomas are present. Laboratory evaluation shows mildly elevated AST (45 U/L) suggesting early alcoholic liver injury, and macrocytic anemia with hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 115 fL, and low serum folate (2 ng/mL), likely related to alcohol use and/or achalasia-associated malabsorption. The patient also has Type 2 diabetes mellitus, gout with elevated serum uric acid (9.2 mg/dL), and history of nephrolithiasis with uric acid crystals in urine. Current medications include metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. The patient presents with recurrent gout flares and has had recent ED visits for flank pain likely related to nephrolithiasis.

This 3-year-old male presents with recurrent acute otitis media, with the most recent episode diagnosed on 2020-01-15 and a follow-up ED visit on 2020-02-15 for worsening right ear pain and fever. The patient's medical history is significant for recurrent acute otitis media requiring multiple antibiotic courses. Family history is notable for a father with history of recurrent otitis media and tympanostomy tubes as a child, and a paternal uncle with chronic eustachian tube dysfunction. During the ED visit, the patient presented with fever (38.9°C), and otoscopic examination revealed a bulging and erythematous right tympanic membrane with tenderness and erythema over the right mastoid process, raising concern for possible mastoiditis. Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (WBC 15,000/mm³) and elevated C-reactive protein (40 mg/L), consistent with bacterial infection. The patient is currently managed with acetaminophen suspension for pain and fever control, with no known drug allergies. No comorbidities beyond the recurrent otitis media are documented. From an Otolaryngology perspective, this patient requires close monitoring for complications of recurrent otitis media and consideration of tympanostomy tube placement given the family history and recurrent nature of his infections.

This 57-year-old female patient has osteopenia as her only active orthopedics-related problem. She has a history of Stage IIA estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer with metastatic disease to liver and adrenal glands, treated with adjuvant endocrine therapy including tamoxifen 20 mg daily. Her medications relevant to orthopedics care include tamoxifen (a SERM that can affect bone mineral density), calcium carbonate with vitamin D3 supplementation (600 mg/400 IU BID), and ibuprofen 400 mg Q8H PRN for pain. She also takes estradiol 1 mg daily for hormone replacement. Laboratory evaluation shows normal calcium and vitamin D levels with no evidence of bone metastases from her breast cancer. The patient has no recent orthopedic encounters or complaints of joint pain, back pain, or fractures. Her osteopenia requires ongoing monitoring and bone health optimization, particularly given her tamoxifen therapy and perimenopausal status.

This 28-year-old male patient has a history of traumatic splenic laceration (occult) diagnosed following a motor vehicle collision in July 2020, and Bacillus cereus food poisoning from reheated fried rice in January 2020. He presented to the ED in March 2021 with severe watery diarrhea after returning from a humanitarian trip to Bangladesh, with vitals showing hypotension (90/54 mmHg) and tachycardia (116/min), and physical exam findings of dehydration with dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill. Laboratory evaluation during the splenic injury workup showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 39.5%) and elevated lactate (2.8 mmol/L), though the FAST ultrasound was negative for free fluid. The patient takes no medications and has no known drug allergies. From a General/Surgery perspective, the key concerns are the occult splenic laceration requiring monitoring for delayed complications such as delayed hemorrhage or splenic rupture, and the recurrent gastrointestinal issues including food poisoning and recent traveler's diarrhea. The patient's social history includes being a graduate student pursuing a Master of Public Health, with no smoking history and social alcohol use.

This 24-year-old female patient has Borderline Personality Disorder as her active psychiatry problem, diagnosed in January 2020. She presents with classic BPD features including unstable interpersonal relationships characterized by idealization and devaluation, intense fear of abandonment, chronic feelings of emptiness, and recurrent self-injurious behavior with forearm cutting. Her medical comorbidities include Irritable Bowel Syndrome and recurrent urinary tract infections, which are not directly psychiatric but are documented in her active problem list. The patient is currently taking no medications. Laboratory results are generally within normal limits, with a urine toxicology screen positive for benzodiazepines noted in January 2020. Family history is significant for maternal major depressive disorder, paternal alcohol use disorder, and a first-degree cousin with Borderline Personality Disorder. Recent encounters demonstrate ongoing psychiatric instability with multiple ED visits for self-harm and overdose attempts following interpersonal conflicts.

This patient is a male with X-linked immunodeficiency (Hyper-IgM syndrome), a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by absent CD40 ligand expression on activated T cells, resulting in elevated serum IgM with low IgA and IgG levels. The patient has a complex medical history including Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (von Gierke disease), Mucolipidosis type II (I-cell disease), Hirschsprung disease, galactosemia, and ventricular septal defect. From a Hematology/Oncology perspective, the most relevant active problem is the Hyper-IgM syndrome, which has led to recurrent infections including pneumonia and otitis media requiring ongoing immunologic management. The patient is currently receiving intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) at 400 mg/kg every 4 weeks as the primary immunomodulatory therapy for his immunodeficiency. Laboratory findings consistent with his immunodeficiency include elevated IgM, low IgA and IgG, and absent CD40 ligand expression. Additional labs show elevated lactic acid (7 mmol/L), uric acid (8 mg/dL), and triglycerides (300 mg/dL) related to his metabolic disorders. The patient has no evidence of hematologic malignancy or cytopenias, with normal platelet count (250,000/mm³) and hemoglobin (11.2 g/dL). His immunodeficiency management requires careful coordination with metabolic disease management, particularly given his galactose intolerance and need for galactose-free formula.

This 58-year-old female with history of severe osteoarthritis of the right hip, osteoporosis, hypertension, and hypothyroidism presented to the hospital for elective right hip arthroplasty. During intraoperative blood transfusion, she developed acute dyspnea and hypoxia with oxygen saturation dropping to 81% on room air, and chest X-ray revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates without cardiomegaly or volume overload. Laboratory evaluation showed normal mucosal immunoglobulin levels and negative Coombs test, consistent with transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI). On postoperative day 2, she presented with increased somnolence and difficulty arousing, with respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. Physical examination revealed mild bibasilar crackles, and chest X-ray showed mild bibasilar atelectasis without consolidation. Laboratory studies demonstrated no significant leukocytosis and normal D-dimer, helping to exclude infection and pulmonary embolism. Morphine for pain control was identified as a contributing factor to her somnolence. Current home medications include lisinopril for hypertension, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, alendronate for osteoporosis, and acetaminophen for pain. The patient has no known drug allergies and is a never smoker with social alcohol use.

This 6-year-old female patient presents with a history of recurrent Group A Streptococcal infection, specifically Scarlet fever. In January 2020, she was evaluated in the ED for high fever (39.4°C), sore throat, chills, and reduced oral intake. Physical examination revealed tonsillar erythema with exudates, strawberry tongue, and a characteristic sandpaper-like erythematous rash on the trunk and axillae. Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis with WBC 12,000/mm³ and neutrophilia at 70%. Rapid antigen detection testing for Group A Streptococcus was positive, confirming the diagnosis of Scarlet fever. In September 2020, she returned with similar symptoms including high fever (39.1°C), sore throat, and a rough red rash over the chest and back, suggesting recurrent or persistent Group A Strep infection. The active problem list identifies "Bacterial infection (Scarlet fever)" diagnosed on 2020-01-15. The patient has no known drug allergies, which is important for antibiotic management. Her past medical history is otherwise unremarkable, she is up to date with vaccinations, and there is no family history of rheumatic heart disease or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Current medications are limited to a pediatric multivitamin. From an Infectious/Disease perspective, this patient requires ongoing evaluation for recurrent Group A Streptococcal infections and appropriate antibiotic therapy to prevent complications such as rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal sequelae.

This 15-year-old male patient presents with a history of mild depressive episode amenable to psychotherapy alone, diagnosed on 2020-05-15 during a routine health maintenance visit. The depression was identified following parental concerns about behavioral changes including declining grades, increased secrecy, and suspected substance use, though the patient denied any drug use during a private conversation. Family history is significant for paternal major depressive disorder. The patient has no current psychiatric medications and takes no medications overall. Comorbid medical conditions include left-sided varicocele diagnosed in 2020-01-15 and osteosarcoma diagnosed on 2020-10-15. Laboratory studies relevant to his overall care show elevated alkaline phosphatase (250 U/L), elevated ESR (40 mm/hr), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase, consistent with his osteosarcoma diagnosis. The patient is a high school student and competitive athlete with no substance use history confirmed. Social history is notable for never smoking and no alcohol use.

This 71-year-old male with a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction presents with recurrent episodes of acute decompensated heart failure, including recent ED visits in January and July 2021 for worsening shortness of breath, orthopnea, and pulmonary edema. His active cardiology problems include heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and hypertension, with significant comorbidities of type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. Cardiology-relevant laboratory findings demonstrate elevated BNP levels of 900 pg/mL consistent with heart failure, elevated creatinine (1.4-1.8 mg/dL) reflecting renal dysfunction, and evidence of volume overload. Current cardiology-directed medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily for afterload reduction and renal protection, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily for rate control and mortality benefit in HFrEF, atorvastatin 40 mg daily for lipid management, aspirin 81 mg daily for antiplatelet therapy, and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for diuresis. Imaging studies consistently demonstrate cardiomegaly with pulmonary vascular congestion and Kerley B lines on chest radiography, while ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Physical examination reveals classic signs of heart failure including elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pulmonary rales, S3 gallop, and bilateral lower extremity edema. The patient has a strong family history of cardiovascular disease with his father experiencing myocardial infarction at age 66 and his brother having coronary artery disease.

This 68-year-old male with Parkinson Disease presents with active psychiatric problems including Parkinson Disease Psychosis (diagnosed 2020) and Major Depressive Disorder (diagnosed 2021), along with Parkinson Disease Dementia (diagnosed 2026). His recent ED presentation on 2026-09-15 with sudden-onset confusion, high fever (39.2°C), severe muscle rigidity, agitation, and hyperreflexia is concerning for a medication-related adverse event, possibly neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome. The patient is currently taking carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg four times daily, ropinirole 0.5 mg three times daily, rasagiline 1 mg daily, and sertraline 50 mg daily for depression. Ropinirole, a dopamine agonist, is known to potentially exacerbate psychosis in Parkinson Disease. His psychiatric history includes persistent sadness, loss of interest, and occasional suicidal ideation in 2021, for which sertraline was initiated. Laboratory evaluation shows normal thyroid function (TSH 2.5 µIU/mL) and normal vitamin B12 (400 pg/mL), ruling out common metabolic causes of psychiatric symptoms. Family history includes Parkinson Disease in his father and late-onset Alzheimer Disease in his mother. The patient's psychiatric care requires careful monitoring of dopaminergic medications for psychosis exacerbation and consideration of antidepressant optimization given his comorbid depression and cognitive decline.

This 44-year-old female patient has HIV infection with AIDS (CD4 < 200) as her primary active infectious disease problem, with severely suppressed CD4 counts ranging from 70-86 cells/μL on recent laboratory testing. She has a comorbid diagnosis of opioid use disorder, currently in sustained remission on maintenance pharmacotherapy. Her antiretroviral regimen includes bictegravir-tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine, and she is on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii prevention. Recent emergency department encounters in 2020 and 2021 presented with progressive neurological symptoms including blurred vision, photophobia, floaters, confusion, headache, and lethargy, which are concerning for opportunistic CNS infections given her severely immunocompromised state. The patient has no documented drug allergies. From an infectious disease perspective, this patient requires ongoing monitoring for opportunistic infections, particularly CNS pathogens given her CD4 count < 100 cells/μL, and optimization of antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function.

This 27-year-old male patient has active Gastroenterology problems including primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and extensive ulcerative colitis (pancolitis), diagnosed in 2020. The PSC-UC association is a well-recognized inflammatory bowel disease-hepatobiliary disease connection. The patient is currently on Ursodiol 300 mg PO three times daily for PSC management. Relevant laboratory findings demonstrate chronic inflammation with elevated CRP (24 mg/L) and ESR (45 mm/hr) in 2020, with worsening anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL in 2023), leukopenia (WBC 2,200/mm³), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 85,000/mm³) in the most recent encounter. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated, consistent with PSC. The patient has significant comorbidities including pemphigus vulgaris (diagnosed 2020) and histoplasmosis (diagnosed 2022). Family history is notable for maternal uncle with ulcerative colitis and mother with rheumatoid arthritis, supporting a genetic predisposition to autoimmune conditions. The patient has no drug allergies and maintains a healthy lifestyle with minimal alcohol use due to his hepatobiliary condition.

This 32-year-old female patient with Bipolar I Disorder presents with recurrent manic episodes and catatonia. Her active psychiatric problems include Bipolar Disorder (diagnosed 2020-01-15), Bipolar I Disorder current episode manic without psychotic features (diagnosed 2024-01-15), and Catatonia (diagnosed 2024-02-15). She has a significant comorbidity of drug-induced hypothyroidism secondary to lithium therapy, diagnosed in 2020-07-15, which manifested with fatigue, constipation, dry skin, and cold intolerance. The patient is currently maintained on lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily, with therapeutic serum lithium levels of 0.8 mEq/L documented in 2020. Recent laboratory monitoring shows normal thyroid-stimulating hormone levels (2.5 μIU/mL in 2024), indicating stable thyroid function. Her family history is significant for Bipolar I disorder in her father and major depressive disorder in her mother. The patient has experienced multiple psychiatric hospitalizations, including a 2024 inpatient admission for catatonia presenting with mutism and refusal to eat, and a 2028 ED visit for manic symptoms with pressured speech and insomnia. She has no substance use disorder, with negative urine toxicology screens, and no known drug allergies.

This 68-year-old male patient has a history of right-sided colon cancer diagnosed in January 2020, status post right hemicolectomy, with no current active Hematology/Oncology problems. His active medical problems include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. The patient has experienced multiple postoperative respiratory complications, including post-obstructive atelectasis, transfusion-related acute lung injury, and opioid-induced respiratory depression following abdominal surgeries. Recent laboratory findings demonstrate anemia with hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, microcytic indices (MCV 72 fL), and iron deficiency (serum iron 30 µg/dL, ferritin 20 ng/mL). Current medications include tiotropium, fluticasone/salmeterol, and albuterol for COPD management; lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension; and metformin for diabetes. The patient has no known drug allergies and has a family history of colorectal cancer in his father.

This 55-year-old male patient presents with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), diagnosed in July 2022 following a 6-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough. Pulmonary evaluation revealed bilateral end-inspiratory crackles on auscultation, oxygen saturation of 94% on room air, and arterial blood gas showing PaO2 of 75 mmHg. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated characteristic subpleural reticular changes and honeycombing without significant lymphadenopathy, consistent with IPF. Pulmonary function tests confirmed a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusion capacity. The patient has significant comorbidities including hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, stable angina pectoris, and renal artery stenosis. His social history is notable for a 30-pack-year smoking history and construction work. Current medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Recent laboratory studies show normal hemoglobin (14.5 g/dL) and renal function (creatinine 1.0 mg/dL), with negative autoimmune markers (ANA and RF). The patient's respiratory status requires ongoing monitoring given the progressive nature of IPF and his cardiovascular comorbidities.

This 53-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed 2020), hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and Class II obesity presents with multiple endocrinology-relevant comorbidities requiring ongoing management. His diabetes is poorly controlled with HbA1c ranging from 6.8% to 7.8% over recent years despite metformin 1000 mg BID therapy. He has significant dyslipidemia with elevated triglycerides (up to 800 mg/dL in 2023), low HDL (35-40 mg/dL), and elevated LDL (130-140 mg/dL). Additional endocrine/metabolic issues include hyperzincemia (diagnosed 2020) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (diagnosed 2022), both related to his obesity. Current medications include metformin for diabetes, atorvastatin 40 mg daily for hyperlipidemia, and antihypertensives (lisinopril 20 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg). Recent labs show elevated uric acid (8.5 mg/dL) and inflammatory markers, consistent with his recent gout presentation. The patient requires comprehensive endocrinology management for glycemic control, lipid optimization, and monitoring of metabolic complications including obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

This 6-year-old male with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, tuberous sclerosis complex, refractory epilepsy, and global developmental delay presents with painless gross hematuria. His active Gastroenterology-relevant problems include history of nephrolithiasis, which is a significant concern given his metabolic disorder. The patient is currently on Allopurinol 50 mg PO daily for uric acid management, which is relevant to his history of kidney stones and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Recent laboratory evaluation shows urinalysis with red blood cells >50 per high power field, consistent with hematuria likely related to his nephrolithiasis history, while serum creatinine (0.6 mg/dL), calcium (9.8 mg/dL), and uric acid (5.2 mg/dL) are within normal limits. His antiepileptic medications (Levetiracetam, Valproic acid, Gabapentin) are not directly GI-related but are important for his overall management. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, a metabolic disorder, can have gastrointestinal manifestations and requires monitoring for metabolic complications. Tuberous sclerosis complex may also have GI involvement including hamartomas. The patient's recent ED visit for hematuria warrants continued urologic/GI surveillance for stone recurrence and evaluation of potential GI manifestations of his underlying syndromes.

This 32-year-old female patient presents with recurrent episodes of fever, headache, confusion, and seizures over a 15-month period. The initial presentation on 2020-01-15 was characterized by fever (38.9°C), headache, confusion, and vomiting, with CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis (250 WBC/µL, 90% lymphocytes), elevated protein (50 mg/dL), and normal glucose. MRI on 2020-07-15 demonstrated increased T2 signal intensity in the left temporal lobe with surrounding edema, classic for herpes simplex encephalitis. The patient was diagnosed with herpes simplex encephalitis on 2020-01-15 but has not received antiviral therapy. She has returned for two subsequent episodes in July 2020 and January 2021 with similar clinical and CSF findings, including temporal lobe involvement on imaging. The patient has no active comorbidities, takes no medications, and has no drug allergies. From an Infectious/Disease perspective, this represents recurrent untreated herpes simplex encephalitis, a medical emergency that typically requires prompt acyclovir therapy to prevent mortality and neurological sequelae. The absence of antiviral treatment despite confirmed diagnosis is a significant concern for disease progression and recurrence.

This 67-year-old male with moderate to severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and current tobacco use disorder (40 pack-year history, currently smoking 0.5 packs/day) presented to the Emergency Department on 2020-07-15 with a 2-day history of progressive shortness of breath and productive cough with yellow sputum, consistent with recurrent COPD exacerbation. His active Emergency/Medicine problems include COPD exacerbation, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to excess normal saline infusion, and atrial fibrillation. On presentation, he was tachypneic (RR 28/min) with hypoxemia (O2 saturation 89% on room air), tachycardia (HR 130 bpm), and hypertension (BP 145/85 mmHg). Physical examination revealed diffuse wheezes and crackles at the lung bases with irregularly irregular heart rhythm. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated respiratory acidosis with pH 7.32, PaCO2 55 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg, and HCO3- 26 mEq/L. ECG showed atrial fibrillation without acute ischemia. His home medications include fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler twice daily, albuterol as needed for dyspnea, and tiotropium once daily. He has no known drug allergies. Family history is significant for lung cancer in his father and COPD in his sibling. This patient requires ongoing management of his COPD exacerbation, respiratory acidosis, and atrial fibrillation in the Emergency/Medicine setting.
